task.goal: Produce a multi-slide 'juxtaposition' editorial carousel that reframes a subject by contrasting an expected dominant narrative against an under-told creative-identity narrative, using highlighted-plate captions, annotated symbol callouts, collaged evidence panels, and a closing explanatory diagram — with no video, no animation, and no single-frame collapse.
task.success_condition: Every slide reads standalone at mobile scale; the highlighted-text caption plates remain the dominant visual surface over any background photography or collage; annotation arrows connecting a garment or symbol to its referent stay legible and subordinate to the caption plates; the closing flow-diagram slide reads as an explanatory model rather than a statistical claim; and the sign-off slide keeps a first-person, unpolished authorial voice instead of collapsing into brand copy.
task.atomic_boundary: One juxtaposition premise (dominant narrative vs. under-told narrative) becomes one ordered, static multi-slide image sequence (this specimen: 12 slides). No video, no motion or animation, no single-frame SuperVisual collapse, and no more than one juxtaposition thesis per carousel.

source_expression_moment.description: The core juxtaposition premise driving the carousel: the contrast this sequence exists to reframe (expected dominant narrative vs. the under-told narrative it is weighed against).

voice_context.description: Voice, tone, and caption-plate typographic context governing rendering decisions across every slide in the sequence, including the closing first-person sign-off register.

slide_source_sequence.description: Ordered reference photography, diagram content, and/or supporting material for each slide, in render order.

carousel_slide_sequence.description: An ordered list of production-ready slide frames (image or diagram plus caption-plate composition) forming one complete carousel post.

activative_input.hidden_pressure: The viewer already has a mental slot for 'DR Congo at the World Cup' pre-filled by decades of conflict-and-crisis coverage; this carousel has to displace that slot with a self-authored creative-identity narrative before the reader's attention lapses past slide two.
activative_input.stance: Observational and self-aware — argues a genuine reframe while admitting its own possible cynicism ('I think it was a set up, but hey').
stakes: the reframe reads as spin instead of a genuine cultural argument
the closing diagram is mistaken for a data claim instead of an explanatory model
the personal authorial voice gets sanded into generic brand copy
identity_urges: be seen as more than a stereotype
get credit for authorship, not just spectacle
activative_input.participation_design: The viewer follows a five-beat arc — hook, contrast setup, symbol callout, evidence collage, explanatory model — then is released on a low-key, first-person sign-off with no hard call-to-action.
activative_input.intended_reaction: The viewer starts searching for more about the subject (the designer, the culture, the country) instead of scrolling past.
activative_input.smallest_useful_commitment: Read past the cover slide instead of scrolling on.
wrong_reading_locks: Do not let the annotation-arrow callouts (garment detail to symbolic referent, e.g. leopard motif to cheetah) assert a specific cultural or historical meaning as verified fact — render them as an interpretive prompt, not a sourced claim, unless the operator supplies a citable source.

Do not let the 'fashion vs. football' juxtaposition read as diminishing the team's athletic legitimacy or as mockery — the reframe argues fashion is a parallel strategic asset, not a replacement for or admission of competitive weakness.

Do not present the stacked rhetorical-question slide ('Who designed them?', 'What's happening in DR Congo?') as verified interview quotes or sourced reporting — it is a framing device simulating audience curiosity, not attributed quotation.

Do not attribute statements, endorsement, or participation in this narrative to any real, identifiable person who appears in comparison photography (e.g. a rival team's player) beyond what is factually documented — contrast photography is contextual, not implied collaboration or quotation.

Do not render the closing flow-diagram slide ('Self, Other, Synthesis') as a statistically validated economic or cultural pipeline — it is an explanatory narrative model and must read as argument, not measured data.
Do not smooth the closing sign-off slide into polished brand voice — the casual, first-person, imperfect tone is load-bearing for the format's authorship thesis and must not be normalized away.
wrong_reading_locks_meaning: Do not substitute the reference specimens with generic fashion stock imagery -- doing so breaks PRM-HUM-009 recognition mechanics by destroying regional cultural specificity.
Do not frame the comparison as moral judgment -- PRM-PSY-018 requires neutral participant observation.
